Chapter 7: Hope as a Practice—Cultivating Light in Dark Times.
You know, we hear the word “hope” all the time. But if you’ve ever been in the middle of a tough season, you know hope can feel really far away. It’s not something you can just summon at will, and it definitely doesn’t stick around on its own.
The truth is, hope isn’t a guarantee—it’s something you have to nurture. It’s a practice, not a promise.
Let me tell you about a father, stuck in the slow haze of recovery after surgery. Night after night, he stared at the ceiling, weighed down by uncertainty. The days just kind of blurred together. Then, one evening, his daughter brought him a simple drawing—a big, bright sun, little stick figures holding hands, and the words, “We love you.” That picture didn’t magically heal him or make his problems disappear. But it did shift something deep inside.
He pinned it to the wall, a small reminder that he was loved—and that even in the middle of difficulty, there’s still beauty to be found.
Most of us imagine hope as this sudden rush of optimism. But honestly, hope is a lot quieter than that. It’s choosing to look for the good, even on the hardest days. It’s the gentle belief that things can get better, even just a little. For some people, hope comes from faith or spirituality. For others, it’s found in nature, in art, or just in the kindness of a friend.
I’m reminded of a woman living with a progressive illness. She started a tiny garden right on her windowsill. Every morning, she’d check on those little green shoots, amazed by how they kept reaching for the light. Those plants became a symbol for her—growth was slow, setbacks happened, but life kept finding a way forward.
Tending to something outside herself gave her comfort and a sense of purpose that her illness couldn’t take away.
Hope doesn’t erase pain or difficulty. It sits beside them, like a quiet companion. You’ll often find that hope shows up where you least expect it—a shared laugh, your favorite song, a moment of real connection with someone else.
And over time, hope can actually become a habit—a way of seeing the world that makes every struggle feel just a little bit lighter.
